title: Old Habits Die Hard: How Conversational History Geometrically Traps LLMs
claim: Observed behavioral persistence across context states is explained by a geometric separation of latent representations, linking probabilistic and geometric views.
layout: 3 columns, left-to-right: example dialogue, then two stacked perspective panels with takeaways
description: On the left, a three-turn question-answer dialogue uses gray speech bubbles for user questions (capitals of Germany, France, USA) and green or red bubbles for model answers (Berlin correct, Rome and New York wrong). Small user and robot icons sit beside the bubbles. Each answer feeds by arrow into a circular state node, φ- (green) or φ+ (red), with curved arrows linking the turns. Two gray arrows labeled 'Estimate phenomenon state transition probabilities' and 'Compute orthogonality of phenomenon representations' lead to two rounded panels on the right. The top panel, 'Probabilistic perspective', shows a two-state Markov chain with thick self-loops, in green for s_φ- and red for s_φ+. The bottom panel, 'Geometric perspective', shows two vectors, h_φ+ (red) and h_φ- (green), separated by an angle θ_ref. Dashed arrows point to takeaway text about self-loops, large angles and carryover effects.
caption: The geometric trap of past context. We correlate external behavior with latent geometry to evaluate the extent of carryover effects. The probabilistic perspective (§3) measures the model’s state consistency, while the geometric perspective (§4) measures the orthogonality and dynamics of latent phenomenon state representations. We find that probabilistic consistency correlates with the geometric trap, where the phenomenon states are separated by a large angle. Samples are illustrative and do not pertain to real data.
abstract: How does the conversational past of large language models (LLMs) influence their future performance? Recent work suggests that LLMs are affected by their conversational history in unexpected ways. For instance, hallucinations in prior interactions may influence subsequent model responses. In this work, we introduce History-Echoes, a framework that investigates how conversational history biases subsequent generations. The framework explores this bias from two perspectives: probabilistically, we model conversations as Markov chains to quantify state consistency; geometrically, we measure the consistency of consecutive hidden representations. Across three model families and six datasets spanning diverse phenomena, our analysis reveals a strong correlation between the two perspectives. By bridging these perspectives, we demonstrate that behavioral persistence manifests as a geometric trap, where gaps in the latent space confine the model's trajectory. Code available at https://github.com/technion-cs-nlp/OldHabitsDieHard.
